chapters.title: Chapter 1: Federal Criminal Securities Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1348)
chapters.description: Introduces the criminal securities fraud statute, its elements, and how it operates in connection with the purchase or sale of securities.
subtopics: Statutory text and structure of §1348(1) and §1348(2)
Elements: scheme to defraud; material misrepresentation or omission; in-connection-with requirement; intent to defraud
Materiality: reasonable investor standard
The “in connection with” nexus to securities transactions
Comparisons and contrasts with SEC Rule 10b-5 (civil vs. criminal; overlap and differences)
Good-faith defense and limits (e.g., puffery vs. false statements)

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Conspiracy to Commit Securities Fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349)
chapters.description: Explains the federal conspiracy provision applicable to fraud offenses and how it attaches to §1348.
subtopics: Statutory framework of §1349 and comparison to 18 U.S.C. §371
Elements: agreement, intent to commit the underlying offense, and knowing participation
Overt act requirement (or lack thereof) under §1349
Scope, withdrawal, and Pinkerton principles (background)
Sentencing exposure tied to the underlying offense

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Aiding and Abetting Liability (18 U.S.C. § 2)
chapters.description: Covers derivative liability for those who facilitate or cause the commission of federal offenses, including securities fraud.
subtopics: Elements: association with venture, participation, and intent to facilitate
Proof via circumstantial evidence and inferences
Distinguishing aiding and abetting from conspiracy
Liability for acts of principals and foreseeability

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Mail and Wire Fraud Doctrines as Foundations for §1348
chapters.description: Surveys core mail and wire fraud concepts that courts use to construe §1348.
subtopics: Elements of 18 U.S.C. §§1341 and 1343
Scheme to defraud and obtaining money or property
Material misrepresentations, omissions, and half-truths
Property versus intangible-rights theories; honest-services limits
No reliance or actual loss requirement in criminal fraud
Doctrinal cross-pollination: using §1341/§1343 precedents to interpret §1348

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Intent to Defraud—Mens Rea in Federal Fraud Offenses
chapters.description: Defines the mental state for fraud and how prosecutors prove it.
subtopics: Intent to deceive and intent to cause harm (deprivation of money or property)
Profit motive versus intent to injure: how courts analyze the distinction
Conscious avoidance (willful blindness) and circumstantial proof
Good-faith defense and the boundary with puffery/opinion

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Landmark—Ciminelli v. United States and the Property Requirement
chapters.description: Explains the Supreme Court’s rejection of the right-to-control theory and its emphasis on traditional property interests in federal fraud.
subtopics: Right-to-control theory defined and rejected
Traditional property interests protected by federal fraud statutes
Why deprivation of valuable economic information alone is insufficient
Effects on charging theories, jury instructions, and appellate review

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Landmark—Kousisis v. United States and the Fraudulent-Inducement Theory
chapters.description: Details the Supreme Court’s endorsement of fraudulent inducement as a valid fraud theory and clarifies the role of economic loss.
subtopics: Fraudulent inducement: using material misstatements to procure transfers of money or property
“Obtaining money or property” as an object of the scheme
No net-pecuniary-loss requirement; equal-value exchanges do not negate fraud
Interaction with intent-to-defraud and materiality analyses

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Fifth Circuit Guideposts—Greenlaw, Evans, and Baker
chapters.description: Outlines Fifth Circuit doctrines shaping §1348 prosecutions and the meanings of key fraud elements.
subtopics: Greenlaw: importing mail/wire fraud concepts into §1348; elemental framework
Evans: defining scheme to defraud and intent to defraud (intent to deceive and cause harm)
Baker: no mirror-image loss/gain requirement
Implications for pleading, proof, and jury instructions in fraud cases

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Market Misstatements and Manipulation—General Securities-Law Background
chapters.description: Provides a primer on common forms of securities fraud and how material statements affect market trading.
subtopics: Categories of securities fraud: misstatements/omissions vs. manipulation
Materiality in securities contexts and the reasonable investor
Public communications and market impact, including social media
Opinions, predictions, and statements of fact—where liability can attach
“In connection with” the purchase or sale: breadth and limits

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Federal Criminal Pleading—Indictment Sufficiency and Motions to Dismiss
chapters.description: Covers what an indictment must contain, how courts evaluate sufficiency, and when dismissal is appropriate.
subtopics: Rule 7(c)(1): plain, concise, and definite statement of the essential facts
Functions of an indictment: elements, fair notice, and double-jeopardy protection
Evaluating sufficiency: taking allegations as true; no evidentiary weighing at Rule 12 stage
Rule 12(b)(3)(B): timing and grounds for pretrial challenges
Particularity in pleading fraud: alleging scheme, materiality, and intent

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Appellate Review in Criminal Cases—Government Appeals and Standards
chapters.description: Explains when the government may appeal pretrial rulings and how appellate courts review indictment dismissals.
subtopics: Government appeals of dismissals under 18 U.S.C. §3731
Finality, timing, and preservation considerations
Standards of review: de novo review of indictment sufficiency
Remand procedures and harmless-error concepts

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Evidence and Proof in Fraud Prosecutions (Overview)
chapters.description: Outlines common evidentiary themes in proving securities-related fraud while distinguishing them from pleading standards.
subtopics: Proving materiality and intent through circumstantial evidence
Use of trading records, communications, and expert testimony
Relevance and limits of loss/gain evidence
Jury instructions to address prejudice and complex-market evidence
